concepts.name: Classic Binary Search
concepts.mental_model: Number line: the closed interval [lo, hi] holds every index the target could be at (invariant). Check mid, then write the new interval without mid.
concepts.mnemonic: [lo, hi] both included → while lo <= hi (size hi-lo+1 > 0). Too small → [mid+1, hi]. Too big → [lo, mid-1]. Empty → not found; lo = insert position.

past_mistakes.note: Wrote mid as `lo + hi // 2` — operator precedence makes it lo + (hi//2); must be (lo + hi) // 2 (or lo + (hi - lo) // 2).

concepts.name: Loop Invariants & Boundaries
concepts.mental_model: Number line intervals. Closed [lo, hi]: size hi-lo+1, empty when lo > hi. Half-open [lo, hi): size hi-lo, empty when lo == hi. Floor mid satisfies lo <= mid < hi.
concepts.mnemonic: Same brackets in, same brackets out: write the new interval with the SAME bracket types, excluding mid, then read the pointer off it. [lo,hi) too big → [lo, mid) → hi = mid; too small → [mid+1, hi) → lo = mid+1.

past_mistakes.note: Said lo = mid 'skips the target at the last index'. Actually it never skips — it freezes: floor mid can equal lo, so lo = mid doesn't move → infinite loop (e.g. half-open [1,3], target 5). Second time attributing the lo=mid bug to 'skipping the end' (also pre-test Q3).

Teach-back: said half-open 'keeps mid' with hi = mid. In [lo, mid) mid is EXCLUDED — hi = mid is how you write 'drop mid' when hi is exclusive. Also called half-open 'the lower bound version' (conflated a boundary convention with a problem).

concepts.name: Lower / Upper Bound
concepts.mental_model: Sorted array → predicate is False…False True…True. Binary search finds the first True. lower bound: arr[i] >= t; upper bound: arr[i] > t. Answer lies in [0, n]; never -1.
concepts.mnemonic: Bounds never return -1 — answer is in [0, n]. >= → lower (bisect_left), > → upper (bisect_right). Count of t = upper - lower. Exact search = lower bound + check arr[lo] == t (guard lo < n).

past_mistakes.note: Copied exact-search asserts expecting -1 onto bound functions; bounds return a position in [0, n], never -1.
LC-278: lo = 0 when versions are 1..n → may call isBadVersion(0) (invalid input). Recurring (same as LC-374): set the search interval from the problem's valid domain, here [1, n).

Asked why it's SAFE to never test n in LC-278 [1, n): answered why it's necessary (API error / out of range) instead of why it's correct. Missing idea: answer space is [lo, hi] — hi is the fallback answer; if all of [1, n) are good, n wins by elimination (guaranteed bad).

What-if LC-278 with no guaranteed bad version: said 'turn it into classic exact search'. Classic == search finds ANY match, not the FIRST True, and a predicate has no == to stop on. Fix is bound + verify: widen to [1, n+1) (n+1 = none) or check isBadVersion(lo) after the loop — same pattern as their half-open exact search.

Teach-back: said exact search needs hi = n + 1 'to check the nth element'. Mixed 1-indexed domain (LC-278 versions 1..n → [1, n+1)) with 0-indexed arrays ([0, n) already includes index n-1; n is the 'none' sentinel). Exact search = lower_bound on [0, n) + check lo < n and arr[lo] == t.

concepts.name: Rotated Sorted Array
concepts.mental_model: One break → at least one side of mid is sorted. A sorted side covers one contiguous value range on the number line; target is there iff it lies in that range.
concepts.mnemonic: Match? → Which side sorted (arr[lo] <= arr[mid])? → Target inside its range (both ends)? yes → go there, no → go the other way.

past_mistakes.note: Why arr[lo] <= arr[mid] (not <): said '< returns false and skips the check' — vague. Precisely: with mid == lo, '<' wrongly declares the RIGHT side sorted and range-checks an unsorted side → goes the wrong way. [3,1], target 1 → returns -1.

Two-phase LC-33: pivot loop went back to moving reference nums[lo] (minutes after fixing it in LC-153 with nums[0]) and flipped the branch (>= -> hi=mid) -> pivot always 0. Phase 2 bugs: sliced nums[lo:hi] after loop when hi==lo (empty), slice-relative idx not offset by p, nums[idx] unguarded (idx can be len), `lo > len` never true. Fix: fixed ref nums[0], bisect_left(nums, t, lo, hi) for absolute index without copying, pick side by target >= nums[0].

Teach-back: called pivot 'where the first element of the array lies' — pivot is the index of the MINIMUM (first i with nums[i] < nums[0]). Also blended the two approaches' comparisons: pivot approach compares to fixed nums[0]; one-pass compares to moving arr[lo] (with <=).

concepts.name: Search a 2D Matrix
concepts.mental_model: LC 74 matrix = one sorted number line folded into rows of width COLS. Search flat index [0, ROWS*COLS - 1]; fold back only to read a value.
concepts.mnemonic: Divide by the WIDTH: r, c = divmod(i, COLS). i // COLS = full rows before i; i % COLS = steps into the row. ROWS only sets hi.

Teach the trace + 'lo lands on insert position' (primes Lower Bound). Visuals reworded to interval language. Traced half-open [4,8] target 1 correctly; identified exit lo as insertion point (confident, correct). Invariants teach-back 2026-09-30: solid on closed mid-1 and lo=mid freeze. Gaps: hi described as 'last element of the array' (it's last candidate of current interval); thinks hi = mid keeps mid; conflates half-open with lower bound. Re-ask (old mid ever picked again?): right conclusion, wrong justification — argued 'interval shrinks' (shrinking != excluding mid) and said 'hi = mid or mid - 1' interchangeably. Correct proof: hi only decreases, future mid < hi <= old_mid. Revisit next session. Asked 'why half-open at all?' — good motivation question. Answered: for exact match it adds nothing; it pays off for boundary problems (answer can be n, mid may be the answer, single exit point lo==hi, matches range/slices/bisect). Acknowledged their teach-back intuition ('hi = mid keeps the boundary') is the correct lower-bound view. Swapped implementation task from half-open exact search to half-open lower_bound. Learner reframed on their own: binary search as boundary questions — lower bound (first arr[i] >= t, bisect_left) vs upper bound (first arr[i] > t, bisect_right). Refined to 'first index where predicate flips False→True'. Learner chose to implement: half-open exact search → lower_bound → upper_bound, in binary_search.py. 2026-09-30 impl review: binary_search_half_open (built as lower_bound + arr[lo]==target check, with lo<len guard), lower_bound, higher_bound all correct — fuzzed 20k cases vs bisect. Gap: bound functions have only 1 assert each; copied exact-search asserts commented out because they expected -1 (bounds never return -1). Index-0 case still untested. Fixed bound asserts (all pass); explained lower_bound([1,3],4)=2 correctly as 'n, where anything >= 4 would go'. Invariants marked done; Lower/Upper Bound now current (implemented, needs practice + teach-back). Recommended: LC-35, LC-34, LC-744, LC-278. Solved LC-35, LC-34 (manual + bisect), LC-744 (manual + bisect), LC-278 — all correct. 34/744 also redone with bisect_left/right. Recurring idiom: starting lo at 0 when the domain starts at 1. Bounds teach-back 2026-09-30: lower bound right (exists-or-insert position) but omitted 'FIRST occurrence'; upper bound phrased loosely ('where every element is greater'); 'hi as answer' only covered target>all, not guaranteed-predicate case; confused n+1 (1-indexed domain) with array exact search; did not use False→True framing. Re-ask (0-indexed versions, no guarantee → [0, n), n = none): correct, confident. Bounds marked done; starting Rotated Sorted Array. Nits: duplicate `search` defs in one class (only last one runs on LC); `not x >= y` → `x < y`. Rotated teach-back 2026-10-01: explained pivot+bisect approach well (two sorted segments, pick by target, bisect_left, dup trimming, O(n) worst/O(log n) best). Gaps: pivot definition imprecise; 'mid greater than first' (should be >=, and arr[lo] in one-pass); didn't explain WHY one side is always sorted; both-ends reason vague; didn't say trimming restores the monotone predicate. Why one side sorted: correct 3-case analysis (mid at min / right of min / left of min). Nuance fixed: when mid IS the min, [lo..mid] contains the break (only [mid..hi] sorted) unless lo == mid. Rotated marked done. 2D pre-test Q1: value + (1,2) correct; formula col = i // ROWS (coincidence at i=6) — should be i % COLS; i=7 breaks it. 2D pre-test Q2: correctly said row-flatten breaks monotonicity for LC-240-type matrix; proposed column-flatten — works for the example only by coincidence (columns happen to chain); fails on [[1,4],[5,6]] → 1,5,4,6. Column-major formula given as (i%COLS, i//COLS) — should be (i % ROWS, i // ROWS).
